author: Carlos Martinez
title: Thrustmaster T818 vs MOZA R9: Which mid-tier direct drive wheelbase wins?
description: Both deliver true direct drive feel under $500. Compare force feedback range, build quality, software and real costs to pick the right wheelbase for your budget.

sections.p: The mid-tier direct drive market has tightened. A year ago, choosing between a servo-based wheelbase and a true direct drive felt like picking between different categories. Now the Thrustmaster T818 and MOZA R9 sit in the same price band, both offering genuine direct drive motor feel, force feedback in the ~8-9 N·m range, and the core hardware quality that separates a rig worth using from one that collects dust. The real difference lies in how each company built their product: where Thrustmaster prioritizes compatibility and ecosystem depth, MOZA leans hard on software maturity and out-of-box feel. Neither is objectively better. Both carry distinct trade-offs worth understanding before you spend that money.

sections.h2: Force feedback range and motor feel

sections.p: The T818 produces roughly 8 N·m of peak torque. The MOZA R9 sits near 9 N·m. On paper, the difference sounds negligible. In practice, most drivers don't perceive a meaningful gap at the mid-range torque levels where you'll spend 90 percent of your time. What matters more is how each wheelbase scales feedback as you increase intensity in your settings.

The T818 uses Thrustmaster's proven servo motor architecture. It delivers a smooth, consistent power curve and rarely clips or feels soft at the top end. The MOZA R9 employs a brushless direct drive motor that many users report as slightly more responsive in the mid-range, with a snappier on-ramp when kerbs or curbs engage. Neither feels sluggish. The T818 gives you a solid, linear experience. The MOZA R9 feels fractionally more immediate, particularly on low-force feedback events like track marbles or slight curb bumps.

list: T818: ~8 N·m, servo-based, smooth and predictable across the RPM range.
MOZA R9: ~9 N·m, brushless direct drive, slightly snappier response in the mid-range, particularly on kerb and impact feedback.
Both are quiet under normal use; neither generates the fan noise of an older indirect drive wheelbase.

sections.tip: If you're coming from a mid-range indirect drive wheelbase (like a T300 or older MOZA R5), either of these will feel noticeably more connected. The jump to true direct drive is real. The difference between T818 and R9 is real too, but subtle. Real-world lap times improve because of setup and driver consistency, not because of a 1 N·m gap.
sections.tipLabel: Direct drive feel is most useful in the mid-range

sections.p: Thrustmaster includes a full ecosystem piece in the T818 package: iRacing Profile support, a robust control panel, and integration with their existing lineup of shifters, handbrakes and button boxes. If you already own a Thrustmaster H-shifter or TH8A shifter, the T818 plays nicely with those peripherals over the same connection hub. Customers report that setup across iRacing, Assetto Corsa Competizione and other titles is straightforward. The software is mature and widely documented.

MOZA's software has improved significantly. The MOZA Pit House software now handles most common sim titles well, including iRacing, Assetto Corsa Competizione, and rFactor 2. Base calibration and force feedback mapping are clearer than they were two years ago. Where Thrustmaster still holds an advantage is sheer depth: more presets, more granular community profiles, and longer support for edge-case titles. MOZA's advantage is simplicity. Setup from the box to your first lap takes less clicking and fewer deep-dive setting tweaks.

For compatibility with button boxes and shifters, the MOZA R9 connects via USB directly to your PC, no additional hub required. Thrustmaster's T818 also uses USB but maintains its legacy peripheral ecosystem. If you run a Logitech or Fanatec shifter alongside either wheelbase, you're wiring them separately anyway, so this distinction matters less than it sounds.

olist: Download the appropriate control software: Thrustmaster Control Panel (T818) or MOZA Pit House (MOZA R9).
Connect the wheelbase to a USB 3.0 port on your PC (not a hub; a direct port if possible).
Calibrate the wheel through the software's calibration wizard.
In your sim (iRacing, ACC, etc.), map force feedback and configure rotation range. Most sims auto-detect the wheelbase and load a default profile.
Test in a practice session, then adjust peak force feedback intensity and any fine-tuning in the control software.

sections.h2: Build quality, warranty and long-term reliability

sections.p: Both wheelbases carry a two-year manufacturer warranty and are built to withstand thousands of hours of use. The T818 chassis is all-metal, with a felt-damped motor cavity and robust mounting points. MOZA's R9 uses a similarly rugged aluminum and steel construction. Neither feels flimsy or cost-cut.

Field reports across both platforms show low rates of early failure. The most common wear item on either wheelbase is the quick-release shaft (if you swap wheels often) or the cable connectors, not the motor or electronics. The T818 has been on the market longer and therefore has a larger installed base with years of data. The MOZA R9 is newer but has accumulated enough real-world hours that reliability looks solid. Neither has a notable pattern of premature failure.

Thrustmaster offers parts availability through their official channels. MOZA does the same. If your quick-release wears out or a cable fails, replacement parts are available, though lead times and pricing vary by region.

The T818 and R9 typically sit in a narrow price band: roughly 400 to 500 USD depending on region, sales, and bundling. The T818 sometimes appears in bundles with a metal wheel rim; the MOZA R9 occasionally bundles with entry-level pedals or a wheel rim. Pricing fluctuates during seasonal sales, but neither has a clear cost advantage most of the time.

Value per dollar depends on what you prioritize. If you already own Thrustmaster peripherals or plan to add them, the T818 unlocks more seamless integration. If you're building a fresh rig and want the minimum friction from unboxing to first race, the MOZA R9's software maturity and straightforward setup offer real value. If you pair either wheelbase with a MOZA CSL pedals load-cell, you're looking at a complete entry-level direct drive rig under 700 to 800 USD, which is genuinely competitive.

sections.tip: Don't let bundled wheels, rims, or pedals drive your decision. You'll likely upgrade the wheel rim or pedals within a year or two anyway. Choose the wheelbase that fits your ecosystem and feels good in your hands during a test. The rest scales from there.

sections.p: Choose the Thrustmaster T818 if you already own Thrustmaster shifters, handbrakes or button boxes, or if you strongly prefer a proven ecosystem with extensive community setup profiles. The T818 is a no-regrets choice for streamlined compatibility and predictable, linear force feedback. You'll spend less time troubleshooting and more time driving.

Choose the MOZA R9 if you're starting fresh and want a wheelbase that feels snappier out of the box, with less time spent in control panel tweaking. The R9 pairs exceptionally well with other MOZA gear (like the MOZA SR-P pedals) if you plan to build a complete rig over time. It's also the pick if simplicity and straightforward software matter more to you than deep ecosystem integration.

Both wheelbases will improve your lap times and consistency compared to an indirect drive wheelbase. Both will last for thousands of hours if cared for. Neither makes you faster than practice and setup do. The real difference is the day-to-day experience of reaching for the wheel, sitting down, and feeling like the rig is part of you. Spend 30 seconds thinking about that feeling, and the right choice becomes clear. Check the specs of your current or planned shifter, pedals, and button box. Pick the wheelbase that integrates with what you already have or plan to buy. That's 90 percent of the decision made.

faqs.q: Is the MOZA R9 better for iRacing than the T818?
faqs.a: No meaningful difference. Both wheelbases work flawlessly in iRacing with native profile support. The R9 may feel fractionally more responsive on kerb impacts, but this is a subtle preference, not an advantage. Choose based on your existing ecosystem and software preferences, not iRacing compatibility. Either wheelbase will deliver the direct drive feel that improves precision in oval and road series.

faqs.q: Can I use my old Thrustmaster pedals with the T818?
faqs.a: Yes, if your pedals connect via USB or the legacy Thrustmaster connector. The T818 is USB-based and will recognize standard gaming joystick/pedal input. You'll need to configure the pedals in your sim's control settings, just as you would with any wheelbase. Legacy Thrustmaster pedal connectors may require an adapter depending on your specific pedal model.

Both are quiet under normal driving. The T818 servo motor is slightly more prone to a faint whine at high force feedback intensities, though most users don't notice it in normal play. The MOZA R9 runs silent in most conditions. If you live in an apartment or share your gaming space, neither will trigger complaints from neighbors. Noise is not a deciding factor between these two.

faqs.q: Will either of these wheelbases feel outdated in two years?
faqs.a: No. Direct drive motor technology is mature and not rapidly evolving. The gap between an 8 N·m and 9 N·m wheelbase is already small. Future wheelbases may offer higher torque or fancier features, but both the T818 and R9 will remain viable, competitive rigs for years. Driver consistency and setup matter far more than chasing incremental hardware improvements.
